decision_reason: A1 leaves descending stairs and jumping relatively close, while jumping and treadmill running have the weakest seen-prototype coverage. Add a torso-specific vertical oscillation concept to distinguish repeated whole-body bouncing from predominantly limb-driven motion, using ascending stairs and basketball as transferable seen anchors. Preserve the remaining concepts rather than inventing distinctions: stepper versus cross trainer depends partly on unspecified technique, sitting versus standing depends on observable segment configuration, and the two lying postures should not be distinguished through an assumed smoothness difference. No class-level values or empirical performance are inferred.

attributes.name: motion_intensity
attributes.definition: Overall magnitude and energy of motion within a window, including both linear and rotational components.

attributes.name: cadence
attributes.definition: Rate at which a meaningful periodic motion unit repeats over time. Cadence measures repetitions per unit time, not the total number of repetitions in the recording.

levels.Low: No clear periodic repetition or a slow repetition rate.

attributes.name: smoothness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion changes continuously rather than through sustained rapid fluctuations.

levels.Medium: Moderately smooth motion with some fluctuations.
levels.High: Continuous and smooth motion with little fluctuation.

attributes.name: impulsiveness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion contains short, abrupt, high-magnitude changes or impacts.

levels.Low: Few or no pronounced abrupt peaks.

attributes.name: posture_inclination
attributes.definition: Average gravity-relative inclination of the global load-bearing body configuration within a window, rather than the orientation of an isolated moving limb.

levels.High: Strongly inclined or nearly horizontal relative to gravity.

attributes.name: posture_variability
attributes.definition: Extent to which the global load-bearing body configuration changes relative to gravity within a window, rather than local limb-orientation changes.

attributes.name: rotational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of angular or rotational motion during the activity.

attributes.name: translational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of sustained linear progression or locomotor translation within a window.

levels.High: Prominent sustained translational or locomotor motion.

attributes.name: motion_regularity
attributes.definition: Temporal consistency and predictability of the motion pattern.

levels.Low: Irregular and poorly predictable motion pattern.
levels.Medium: Partly structured motion with moderate variability.

attributes.name: torso_vertical_oscillation
attributes.definition: Strength of recurring gravity-vertical acceleration and deceleration of the torso associated with whole-body bouncing, excluding static gravity and isolated impact peaks.

levels.Low: Little or no recurring vertical torso acceleration and deceleration.
levels.Medium: Moderate recurring vertical torso acceleration and deceleration.
levels.High: Strong recurring vertical torso acceleration and deceleration.

operations.reason: motion_intensity: G3 supports overall acceleration and rotation magnitude across the available body segments. This retains an effort-related contrast between treadmill walking and running and between stepper and cross trainer. Speed, resistance and technique can overlap, so semantic effort is not assumed to determine signal magnitude exactly.

operations.reason: cadence: G6 supports repetition rate in recurring limb and torso motion. Walking and cycling provide transferable periodic-motion anchors for treadmill running and cross trainer. Step-versus-stride harmonics and freely chosen exercise rates can make ordinal boundaries ambiguous; cadence is not inferred from speed alone.
target_unseen: running on a treadmill with a speed of 8 km/h
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)
cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions

operations.reason: smoothness: G9 supports sustained rapid changes in acceleration or rotation, retaining a continuous-motion versus fluctuating-motion distinction transferable from cycling and stepper to cross trainer and impact-rich activities. Impacts can reduce smoothness, but isolated peaks do not define it. Sensor attachment and technique introduce ambiguity; lying orientation alone does not justify different smoothness.
seen_anchors: cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions

operations.reason: impulsiveness: G10 supports short abrupt changes transmitted through torso and limb sensors. Basketball and stair ascent offer impact-related anchors for jumping, descending stairs and running. Landing style and impact attenuation can change the evidence, and impulsiveness alone cannot reliably separate these unseen activities.
target_unseen: running on a treadmill with a speed of 8 km/h

operations.reason: posture_inclination: G1 supports gravity-relative torso and limb configuration, preserving transfer from standing, lying and stair ascent to sitting and inclined walking. Sitting can retain an upright torso, and treadmill slope does not uniquely determine body lean; an isolated segment must not be treated as the global configuration. No unsupported knee-angle or lying-side attribute is introduced.
target_unseen: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in 15 deg inclined positions)

operations.reason: posture_variability: G12 supports changes in gravity-relative body configuration. Rowing and stable treadmill walking anchor substantial versus limited configuration changes for jumping and inclined walking. Local limb cycles and dynamic acceleration can obscure global posture; vertical bouncing without appreciable reorientation need not imply high posture variability.
target_unseen: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in 15 deg inclined positions)
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)

operations.reason: rotational_motion: G2 supports angular motion directly through the available gyroscopes. Cycling, stepper and rowing provide rotational-motion anchors for cross trainer and running. Arm use and joint excursion vary, so prominent rotation does not uniquely identify an apparatus or imply global posture change.

seen_anchors: cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions

operations.reason: translational_motion: G13 provides short-window translational-motion evidence, preserving the progression concept shared by stair ascent and descent. This is a limited proxy: constant-velocity travel, treadmill locomotion and elevator motion are not uniquely recoverable from inertial signals. Retention avoids replacing a useful concept with an unsupported claim of absolute displacement or vertical travel direction.
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)

operations.reason: motion_regularity: G11 and G6 support recurrence and temporal consistency. Structured treadmill and apparatus exercise contrast with basketball, supporting transfer to running, cross trainer and repeated jumping. Brief windows, transitions and irregular jump timing can weaken this evidence; regularity is distinct from repetition speed.
target_unseen: running on a treadmill with a speed of 8 km/h
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)

operations.reason: torso_vertical_oscillation: G1 supports the gravity reference, G3 and G14 support directional torso acceleration magnitude, and G6 supports recurring rather than isolated motion. Expected evidence is repeated vertical acceleration and deceleration at the torso, not inferred jump height or flight time. This adds a spatially scoped contrast for descending stairs versus jumping and helps relate running and jumping to seen stair ascent and basketball. Trunk lean, soft landings, transmitted foot impacts and basketball windows without bouncing can blur levels; oscillation strength is not assumed to follow impact strength or cadence.

seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)

semantic_redundancy_review: The ten attributes retain distinct physical meanings. Cadence describes repetition speed, whereas regularity describes consistency. Smoothness concerns sustained fluctuations, whereas impulsiveness concerns brief peaks. Mean inclination differs from posture variation, and segment rotation differs from global reorientation. Translation describes progression rather than oscillation. The added torso vertical oscillation attribute concerns recurring, directionally scoped torso acceleration, not whole-body energy, isolated impacts, posture change or net displacement; correlation with intensity and impulsiveness is expected but not definitional redundancy. No apparatus identity, mandatory arm use, bilateral phase relation, absolute velocity or ascent/descent direction is assumed. Close pairs without a stable additional observable distinction are deliberately left unresolved.
